history.heading: Ancient civilisations
paragraphs: Peru was home to Caral, the oldest known city in the Americas, built around 2600 BCE. Later cultures included the Chavín, the Paracas, the Nazca, famous for the giant lines drawn in the desert, the Moche, with their pottery and the tomb of the Lord of Sipán, the Wari and the Chimú, whose capital Chan Chan was the largest adobe city in the world.

history.heading: The Inca Empire
paragraphs: In the 15th century the Inca, based in Cusco, built the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, Tawantinsuyu, stretching from Ecuador to Chile. They built a vast road network and remarkable stone architecture, including Machu Picchu.

Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532 and executed him in 1533. Lima, founded in 1535, became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, centre of Spanish power in South America. Silver mining relied on forced indigenous labour. Túpac Amaru II led a major indigenous rebellion in 1780.

history.heading: Independence and the republic
paragraphs: José de San Martín proclaimed independence in 1821, and Simón Bolívar's forces secured it in 1824. Peru lost territory to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884).

The 20th century saw alternating civilian and military governments. In the 1980s and 1990s, the Shining Path insurgency and state repression killed around 70,000 people. Alberto Fujimori defeated the insurgency but ruled in an authoritarian way and was later imprisoned for human rights abuses and corruption. Since 2016 Peru has had extreme political instability, with many presidents removed; in October 2025 Congress removed President Dina Boluarte.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Spanish is the main language, and Quechua and Aymara are official where they are spoken; Quechua is spoken by millions. The population is mainly mestizo and indigenous, with Afro-Peruvian, European and Asian (Chinese and Japanese) communities. Most people are Catholic, often blending Andean traditions. Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the sun, is celebrated in Cusco.

culture.heading: Food and arts
paragraphs: Peru is considered one of the world's great culinary destinations. Dishes include ceviche, lomo saltado, ají de gallina, and Chinese-Peruvian chifa and Japanese-Peruvian Nikkei cuisine. Peru has thousands of potato varieties, and pisco is the national spirit.
Writers include Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa and César Vallejo. Andean textiles, music with panpipes and the marinera dance are traditions.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Peru is a presidential republic with a unicameral Congress, though a bicameral parliament is being restored from 2026. Politics has been unstable, with a powerful Congress frequently removing presidents, fragmented parties and widespread corruption scandals. Low public trust in institutions is a major concern. General elections were held in April 2026.

economy.heading: Mining and growth
paragraphs: Peru has been one of Latin America's fastest-growing economies since 2000. It is a leading producer of copper, silver, gold and zinc, and mining dominates exports. Agricultural exports such as blueberries, avocados, grapes and asparagus have boomed, along with fishmeal.

Tourism, centred on Machu Picchu and Cusco, is important. The currency, the sol, has been stable thanks to a respected central bank. Informal work, illegal mining and inequality are challenges. The Chancay megaport, built with Chinese investment, opened in 2024.
